summary: Describes the data compression algorithms of the Dacom 450 fax machine in detail and the Dacom 500 briefly. The Dacom 500 was used by the INTELPOST electronic-mail network under development by the US Postal Service and foreign administrators.

plainLanguage.summary: Fax pictures are mostly blank space, so machines squeeze them down. This memo explains how two particular machines do the squeezing and unsqueezing.

subtitle: How two commercial fax machines compress and transmit image data

tldr.problem: Facsimile machines need to compress image data efficiently for transmission, and different manufacturers use different algorithms. The Dacom 450 and 500 are widely used but their compression schemes need documentation for interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The Dacom 450 uses two-dimensional run-length encoding with a finite-state automaton to detect runs of white and black pixels, while the Dacom 500 uses the standardized T.4 (CCITT Group 3) one-dimensional Huffman-coded compression.
tldr.outcome: Software modules for encoding and decoding these formats were implemented, allowing facsimile data to be transcoded between different representations and network services like INTELPOST.

today: RFC 803 describes compression algorithms and software modules from the early 1980s. The Dacom 450's proprietary two-dimensional encoding is now historical, but the CCITT T.4 standard used by the Dacom 500 evolved into modern fax standards (Group 3 and Group 4 facsimile) still used today.

sections.title: Facsimile Machines and Data Compression
sections.content:
The Dacom 450 and 500 are Computerfax facsimile machines used by the DARPA Internet Program and other networks. Like all fax machines, they must compress scanned image data to reduce transmission time and storage requirements. This RFC documents software modules written in PDP-11 MACRO-11 assembly language that encode and decode facsimile data for these machines.

The modules translate between the compressed formats used by the machines and intermediate representations suitable for editing, transmission and archiving: bit-map format (one bit per pixel) and run-length format (pairs of lengths for runs of black and white). The Dacom 500 is particularly important because it was used by the INTELPOST electronic-mail network, a project under development by the US Postal Service and foreign postal administrations.
sections.plainLanguage: Fax machines scan documents into pictures and squeeze them down for sending. These programs convert between the compressed fax format and simpler formats computers can edit and store.

sections.title: Dacom 450: Two-Dimensional Run-Length Encoding
sections.content:
The Dacom 450 scans in high-resolution mode at 1726 pels (pixels) wide by about 2200 lines tall. It uses a clever two-dimensional compression algorithm that encodes two rows of pixels at a time. As the machine scans left-to-right across each pair of rows, it tracks the color of pixels in each column: white-white (state 0), black-white (state 1), white-black (state 2), or black-black (state 3).

The encoding is described as a non-deterministic finite-state automaton (NFSA). When pixels are all one color (states 0 or 3), the encoder uses run-length encoding with an adaptive field width: it counts how many columns in a row share the same color, then transmits the count in a variable-length field (2 to 7 bits). When pixels alternate (states 1 or 2), fixed-length transition codes are sent. This two-dimensional approach compresses fax images better than one-dimensional schemes because it can recognize patterns in both horizontal and vertical directions.
sections.plainLanguage: The Dacom 450 looks at pairs of lines and groups together pixels of the same color. It sends a count of how many pixels in a row are white or black, using different numbers of bits depending on how many bits it needs.

sections.title: Dacom 450: Decoding and Frame Structure
sections.content:
For decoding, the algorithm is expressed as a deterministic finite-state automaton (DFSA) that processes one bit at a time (except for the variable-length run-length codes in states 0 and 3). The DFSA makes the decoding algorithm simpler and faster than the encoding automaton.

Data are organized into 585-bit frames containing a 24-bit synchronization code, a 37-bit leader with control flags and state information, a 512-bit data field, and a 12-bit CRC checksum. The header tracks the current position in the image, the field widths for white and black runs (2 to 7 bits), and the current decoder state. This allows each frame to be self-synchronizing: if a frame is lost or damaged, decoding can resume from the header of the next frame without starting over.

The RFC specifies two file formats: the UCL format (used for DCNET) stores each 585-bit frame in a 76-byte record, and run-length and bit-map formats store decoded data for processing on computers. Run-length pairs use 16-bit words with positive values for white runs and negative two's complement for black runs, with zeros separating lines.
sections.plainLanguage: The decoder reads the compressed bits and reconstructs the original image. Data arrives in chunks with headers that say what state the decoder is in, so if a chunk gets lost, the next one can pick up where the previous one left off.

sections.title: Dacom 500: CCITT T.4 Compression
sections.content:
The Dacom 500 is a faster, high-speed version that transmits at 50 kilobits per second (compared to 2.4-9.6 kbps for the Dacom 450). Rather than a proprietary algorithm, it implements the CCITT T.4 standard for Group 3 facsimile compression, which is one-dimensional run-length encoding with Huffman coding.

The T.4 algorithm represents run lengths using a binary tree of Huffman codes. Different code sequences represent black and white run lengths (such as 1, 2, 64, or 1728 pixels). The Dacom 500 decoder traverses the appropriate tree (black or white) bit-by-bit from the input, accumulating run length values until reaching a terminal node. The encoder performs the reverse: it scans the bitmap, counts runs of pixels, and looks up the corresponding Huffman code for each run length.

Data in T.4 format are stored in 512-byte blocks with a header listing the number of pages and their lengths, followed by page data each preceded by a page-setup command and followed by an end-of-record command. These commands encode the T.4 EOL code and options for vertical resolution, paper length, and document presence.
sections.plainLanguage: The Dacom 500 uses a standard compression method that is simpler and faster: it looks at pixels one line at a time and uses lookup tables to find the best code for each group of same-colored pixels.

sections.title: Format Comparison and Transcoding
sections.content:
The RFC provides empirical data comparing the four main facsimile formats in use: Dacom 450, Dacom 500 (T.4), 16-bit run-length, and bit-map. For a typical test document (INTELP, a composite INTELPOST image with text and graphics), the file sizes vary: T.4 compressed to 193 512-byte blocks, Dacom 500 to 925 blocks, run-length to 413 blocks, and the uncompressed bit-map to 3.8 megabits.

Transcoding between these formats takes measurable time. On an LSI-11/23 processor, converting from T.4 to bit-map takes 95 seconds, from bit-map to Dacom 450 takes 110 seconds, and from run-length to Dacom 450 takes 89 seconds. The RFC notes that T.4 format offers the best compression for most documents, but the choice of format depends on the speed and storage constraints of the system in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Different compression methods create different file sizes. T.4 is the most compact, but conversion between formats takes time depending on how much the image needs to be recompressed.
